source_text: Porro iam satis multa de Genesi. Transeamus ad apostolum Paulum, quem opinionis suae Manichaeus et Traducianus opinantur. Cum ergo de mortuorum resurrectione dissereret, ait: Sicut in Adam omnes moriuntur, ita et in Christo omnes vivificabuntur [n193] . Hoc testimonium usurpasti tu, cum quo nobis causa est; sed quid eo confici putares, quia tu tacuisti, etsi suspicer, tamen confirmare vix possum. Quid enim spectat ad traducem, si omnes in Adam mori dicantur; cum Adam nomen hominis sit, tradux autem peccati et labis Manichaeae indicium? Nisi forte nihil aliud ipsum Adam, quam peccatum et esse, et sonare fatearis; ut hac appellatione Apostolus omnes mori in peccato pronuntiasse videatur? Sed hoc propalam insanum est. Quid igitur novum, si quia Adam sermo hebraeus nihil aliud indicat quam hominem (hoc enim interpretatio ipsius exprimit) dixerit Apostolus: In Adam omnes moriuntur, et in Christo omnes vivificabuntur; id est, secundum hominis qui moriuntur naturam, per virtutem Christi a mortuis excitantur? Huic sententiae qui inficiatur, insanit; eiusdem quippe auctoris virtute, qui in hac vita fecunditatem et mortalitatem instituit, universi excitabuntur e sepulcris, ut recipiat unusquisque propria corporis sui, prout gessit, sive bonum, sive malum [n194] . Hoc itaque dicto Apostoli, quo ait: Sicut in Adam omnes moriuntur, ita et in Christo omnes vivificabuntur; mortem corporalem quae iustis iniustisque communis est, an poenalem illam diabolo et impiis deputatam insinuari putas? Si naturalem istam simplicem, quae in sanctis etiam pretiosa est [n195] , quae non solum bonis et malis, verum etiam hominibus pecudibusque ex aequo accidit; hanc, inquam, mortem hic Apostolus indicavit; manifestum est quoniam nomine Adae naturam humanitatis, nomine autem Christi potentiam creatoris et excitatoris ostendit. Sin autem quod ait: In Adam omnes moriuntur; crimen hic velis intellegi, non naturam; suppetit expositio tam aperta quam certa, videlicet ut dixerit: Sicut omnes, id est, multi Adae imitatione moriuntur; ita omnes, id est, multi Christi imitatione salvantur. Aut ergo de communi morte locutus est, et naturam indicavit; aut de peccato, et imitationem accusavit. Sic enim et post pauca subiunxit: Sicut portavimus - inquit - imaginem terrestris, portemus etiam imaginem illius caelestis [n196] . Certe susceptio imaginis non poterat imperari, si naturalis in qualitate alterutra crederetur.
pass_a_gloss: Further already enough many things about Genesis. Let us pass to the apostle Paul, whom Manichaeus and the Traducian opine of their opinion. When therefore he was discussing about the resurrection of the dead, he says: As in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive. You usurped this testimony, with whom we have a cause; but what you thought was accomplished by it, because you were silent, although I may suspect, nevertheless I can scarcely confirm. For what looks to the tradux, if all are said to die in Adam; when Adam is a name of a human, but the tradux an indication of sin and of Manichaean wasting? Unless perhaps you confess that Adam himself is nothing other than sin, both to be and to sound; so that by this appellation the Apostle may seem to have pronounced that all die in sin? But this is openly insane. What therefore new, if because Adam a Hebrew word indicates nothing other than a human (for this his interpretation expresses) the Apostle said: In Adam all die, and in Christ all will be made alive; that is, according to the nature of the human who die, they are stirred from the dead through the virtue of Christ? He who disowns this sentence is insane; for by the virtue of the same author, who in this life instituted fertility and mortality, all will be stirred from tombs, that each one may receive the things of his own body, according as he did, whether good or evil. By this saying therefore of the Apostle, by which he says: As in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive; do you think a corporal death which is common to the just and the unjust, or that penal one assigned to the devil and the impious, is insinuated? If that simple natural, which even in the holy is precious, which happens equally not only to good and evil, but even to humans and cattle; this death, I say, the Apostle indicated here; it is manifest that by the name of Adam he showed the nature of humanity, but by the name of Christ the power of the creator and stirrer. But if what he says: In Adam all die; you would want a charge understood here, not nature; an exposition so open as certain is available, namely that he said: As all, that is many, die by imitation of Adam; so all, that is many, are saved by imitation of Christ. Either therefore he spoke of a common death, and indicated nature; or of sin, and accused imitation. For thus also after a few things he subjoined: As we have borne, he says, the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of that heavenly. Certainly a taking-up of an image could not be commanded, if it were believed natural in either quality.

pass_b_english: Enough now about Genesis. Let us turn to the apostle Paul, whom Mani and the advocate of inherited sin think supports their opinion. Discussing the resurrection of the dead, he says: ‘As all die in Adam, so all will be made alive in Christ’ (1 Corinthians 15:22) (Psalm 116:15). You, with whom we have our dispute, appropriated this testimony. But because you did not say what you thought it established, I can scarcely confirm it, though I suspect it.

What does it have to do with transmission of sin if everyone is said to die in Adam, when Adam is a human being’s name, while transmission denotes sin and Manichaean corruption? Unless perhaps you acknowledge Adam himself to be and to mean nothing other than sin, so that by this name the apostle seems to have pronounced that everyone dies in sin? But this is obviously insane.

What is strange, then, if, since the Hebrew word Adam means nothing other than ‘human’—as its translation expresses—the apostle said, ‘All die in Adam, and all will be made alive in Christ’: those who die according to human nature are raised from the dead through Christ’s power? Anyone denying this statement is mad. By the power of the same author who established fertility and mortality in this life, everyone will be raised from the graves, ‘so that each may receive what belongs to deeds done in the body, according to what was done, whether good or evil’ (2 Corinthians 5:10).

In the apostle’s saying, then, ‘As all die in Adam, so all will be made alive in Christ,’ do you think he indicates bodily death, common to the just and unjust, or that penal death appointed for the devil and the ungodly? If this ordinary natural death, which in the saints is even precious (Psalm 116:15; LXX/Vulgate Psalm 115:6), and happens equally not only to good and evil people but also to humans and animals—if, I say, the apostle indicates this death—then plainly ‘Adam’ denotes human nature, while ‘Christ’ denotes the power of the Creator who raises the dead.

But if you want ‘All die in Adam’ to mean guilt rather than nature, an explanation is available as plain as it is certain: As all—that is, many—die by imitating Adam, so all—that is, many—are saved by imitating Christ. Either he spoke of common death and indicated nature, or of sin and condemned imitation. So he added shortly afterward: ‘As we have borne the image of the earthly one, let us also bear the image of the heavenly one’ (1 Corinthians 15:49). Certainly assuming the image could not be commanded if it were considered natural in either quality.

choices.why: Julian's polemic target is inherited sin as a natural evil (malum naturale), the vine-layer metaphor, not a later systematic 'original sin' slogan and not soul-traducianism as such.

traducianism of the soul (not the load here)
